title: Lower your voices
hookLine: don't raise your voices above the Prophet's voice (49:2)

lines: A SURAH ABOUT HOW WE TALK.
cards: Two people talking over each other, then three, each a little louder, until nobody is listening and everyone is shouting a point at the ceiling. Usually it's an office or a family dinner.
Once, the reports say, it happened in Medina, in front of the Prophet ﷺ, and the two rising voices belonged to Abu Bakr and 'Umar.
That scene sits behind Surah Al-Hujurat, the Private Rooms, the forty-ninth surah: short, and something like a manual for how a community talks.

teach.b: Verse two, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Lift not up your voices above the voice of the Prophet, nor shout when speaking to him as ye shout one to another."
Then a warning: lest your works be rendered vain while you don't notice. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari gives the occasion.
A delegation came from the tribe of Banu Tamim, and Abu Bakr and 'Umar disagreed about who should be appointed over them. They argued in front of the Prophet until their voices rose.
After this verse, the report says, 'Umar spoke to the Prophet so softly that he sometimes had to be asked to repeat himself. Another Companion took it even harder.

teach.h: THABIT, LOUD BY NATURE, STAYED HOME.
teach.b: Thabit ibn Qays had a naturally loud voice; he was the speaker for the Ansar. When the verse came down he stayed home, convinced his deeds were wasted.

The Prophet noticed he was missing, sent someone to ask, and sent back a message: Thabit was not among the people of the fire, but of paradise. The next verse praises those who lower their voices in his presence.
Commentators extend the courtesy beyond his lifetime: raising one's voice over his teaching is a related kind of disrespect.
You may remember Luqman's advice to his son, earlier this year: walk modestly and lower your voice. Two surahs, two settings, the same instinct.
Volume isn't the same as truth. Often it's a sign that listening has stopped.

how: Muslims are taught to speak quietly in mosques, and visitors to the Prophet's mosque in Medina recall this verse at his grave; scholars also apply it to how hadith and his teaching are discussed.

o: the speaker for the Ansar, loud by nature
a Companion whose argument with 'Umar grew loud
the tribe whose delegation came to Medina

games.q: lower your voices — tap the pairs.

s: the verse only matters for people who met the Prophet
commentators extend it to raising one's voice over his teaching.
after the verse, 'Umar spoke so softly he had to repeat himself
Thabit ibn Qays was told he was of the people of paradise
the Prophet sent that message when Thabit feared his deeds were lost.

games.q: you're Thabit ibn Qays, loud by nature. the verse comes down and you're sure your deeds are wasted. what happens?
o: the Prophet notices you're missing and sends good news.
games.why: the Prophet asked after him and sent word that he was of the people of paradise.

practice: Picture the next room you'll be in with other people: a dinner table, a meeting, a group chat with a voice of its own.
Choose one moment there to lower your volume on purpose, especially if you disagree, and let your breath be slow and low now so your body remembers it. If you pray, you can ask for a humble voice.

wordCard.voice: Abu Bakr. His voice, raised with 'Umar's in front of the Prophet, became the reason this verse came down, and he learned to speak so softly he had to repeat himself. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: do not raise your voices (49:2).

carryVoice: Your line: the humble voice. A lower voice leaves room for listening. That's day five hundred eighty-three.
